query_instance_subgraph.input_schema.properties.relation_type_pa: Relation traversal paths used to fetch a subgraph. Value rules for per-node filters: like/not_like take a literal substring (do not add % yourself; an unescaped % is rejected) and regex anchoring and case sensitivity depend on the resource storage (write .*term.* for "contains").
Object type steps and optional conditions in this path.
Object type id for this path step.
Filter condition for instances of this object type.

Filter operator. Comparison operators are derived from the property type and are NOT listed in condition_operations: string-like types (string/keyword/text) support == != in not_in > >= < <= like not_like regex; numeric and date/time types support == != in not_in > >= < <= range out_range but not like/regex; exist/not_exist work on any type and take no value. Index-backed operators follow the property's condition_operations: match needs a full-text index, knn needs a vector index. A property with no condition_operations key simply has no index built - it can still be filtered. multi_match in condition_operations is only a full-text-index marker; use match instead. like/not_like match a literal substring, not a SQL LIKE pattern: pass the text to be contained and do not add % yourself; an unescaped % is rejected (write \% to match the character itself) and _ is an ordinary character. regex anchoring depends on where the resource lives: the index path matches the whole string, while table resources render an unanchored SQL regex (MariaDB `REGEXP`, PostgreSQL `~`) that searches, so write .*term.* for "contains" - correct on both. Case sensitivity follows the same split: the index path is case-sensitive, table resources follow the column collation (the common utf8mb4_*_ci ones are case-insensitive), and it applies to ==, like and regex alike, so never rely on case to filter.
Where the filter value should be sourced from.

Literal filter value. Single value for scalar operators; array for in/not_in; [min, max] for range (both ends inclusive, elements same type); out_range takes the same [min, max] and excludes that closed interval; like/not_like take a literal substring (not a SQL LIKE pattern - do not add % yourself, an unescaped % is rejected, \% matches the character itself); regex takes a pattern whose anchoring and case sensitivity depend on the resource storage (write .*term.* for "contains"); exist/not_exist take no value. knn additionally needs limit_key=k and limit_value.
Sort rules for this object type.
Maximum instances for this object type step.
Relation type hops between object types.

Target object type id for the relation.

explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.kn_id.descriptio: Knowledge network id. Can also be supplied by the X-Kn-ID request header.

explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.direction.descri: Direction to explore. forward follows relations as declared, backward follows them in reverse, bidirectional follows both. Use bidirectional when you are unsure how the relation was modelled.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.path_length.desc: Maximum number of hops, 1 to 3; anything higher returns a 400. Path counts grow fast with depth, so start at 1 or 2 and raise it only if the answer is not there.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.condition.descri: Filter on the SOURCE object type only; it does not constrain the other object types along a path. Same structure as query_object_instance's condition. Omit it to start from every instance of the source type, subject to limit.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.condition.proper: Field name (a property of the source object type).
Filter operator, same rules as query_object_instance: comparison operators follow the property type, while match and knn depend on the property's condition_operations.
Value source; only const is supported.
Field value; a single value for scalar operators, an array for in/not_in, [min, max] for range/out_range, omitted for exist/not_exist.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.concept_groups.d: Concept group ids that bound the exploration. Omit for no bound.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.include_incomple: Whether to return partial paths - those that traversed at least one edge but ran out of hops before reaching path_length. Defaults to false. Turn it on to see how far the connection actually goes. Zero-edge paths are never returned.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.limit.descriptio: Maximum number of SOURCE instances to start from, default 10. This is not a cap on returned paths or on total objects.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.sort.description: Sort applied to the SOURCE object type, compared in array order. Together with limit it decides which instances the exploration starts from; it does not order the paths themselves.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.sort.items.prope: Sort field (a property of the source object type).
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.offset.descripti: Offset paging over the SOURCE instances. Mutually exclusive with search_after.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.search_after.des: Cursor paging over the SOURCE instances: pass the search_after from the previous response to get the next batch of starting points. Mutually exclusive with offset.
explore_subgraph.input_schema.properties.include_logic_pa: Whether to include logic property parameters. Defaults to false.
explore_subgraph.output_schema.properties.objects.descrip: Objects that participate in at least one relation, keyed by object id.
explore_subgraph.output_schema.properties.isolated_object: Objects with no relation at all. This is a valid answer, not a failure: it states that those starting points connect to nothing within the given direction and hop count. Do not retry or reword because this is populated.
The concrete relation paths. Each carries a relations array (relation_type_id, source_object_id, target_object_id) and a length in edges. Look objects up by id in objects.
explore_subgraph.output_schema.properties.total_count.des: Total number of SOURCE instances matching the filter, independent of limit, and unrelated to the number of paths or objects returned. No match is 0, present rather than absent. An absent field means no total was computed for this call - which is what happens from the second page onward when paging with search_after - so do not read absence as 0.
explore_subgraph.output_schema.properties.search_after.de: Cursor for the next batch of source instances; empty when the source instances are exhausted.

query_object_instance.input_schema.properties.filters.descript: Legacy flat filters. Prefer condition for new calls. Same operator and value rules as condition: like/not_like take a literal substring (do not add % yourself; an unescaped % is rejected) and regex anchoring and case sensitivity depend on the resource storage (write .*term.* for "contains").
query_object_instance.input_schema.properties.filters.items.pr: Filter operator, same rules as condition.operation: comparison operators come from the property type (like/not_like/regex only on string-like types), match requires condition_operations to contain match. exist/not_exist (no value) and knn (needs limit_key/limit_value) cannot be expressed here - use condition. like/not_like take a literal substring (do not add % yourself; an unescaped % is rejected) and regex anchoring and case sensitivity depend on the resource storage (write .*term.* for "contains").

query_metric.input_schema.properties.kn_id.descriptio: Knowledge network id. The X-Kn-ID request header carries it too.
query_metric.input_schema.properties.metric_id.descri: Metric id, taken from related_metrics[].id of a get_object_types response. Do not invent one.
query_metric.input_schema.properties.time.description: Time window. It may be omitted entirely for a metric with no time dimension, meaning related_metrics[].time_dimension is empty. Note that omitting instant is the same as instant=false, a series query, which requires step. Either give both start and end or neither.
true takes a single point, the current value; false or omitted takes a series, which requires step.
Series step, case insensitive. Required for a series query; ignored downstream when instant=true.
query_metric.input_schema.properties.condition.descri: Filter conditions, shaped exactly like the condition parameter of query_object_instance (field / operation / value / value_from, nestable with and/or).
query_metric.input_schema.properties.analysis_dimensi: Analysis dimensions, which split the result by dimension. The values have to come from related_metrics[].analysis_dimensions.
query_metric.input_schema.properties.limit.descriptio: Maximum number of rows to return
query_metric.input_schema.properties.fill_null.descri: Whether a step with no data is filled with a null in a ranged series query. Defaults to false. It applies to series queries only and needs both time.start and time.end.
query_metric.output_schema.properties.datas.descripti: Result series grouped by labels. Without analysis_dimensions there is usually one entry and labels is empty.
query_metric.output_schema.properties.datas.items.pro: The dimension values of this series
The time points in readable form
Metric values, one per entry in times

Response format: json or toon. Defaults to toon.
read_skill_file.input_schema.properties.skill_id.descrip: Skill id, taken from the skill_id of list_skills or find_skills.
read_skill_file.input_schema.properties.rel_path.descrip: Path relative to the skill package root, taken from files[].rel_path of a get_skill_content response. A path outside the package is rejected, ../ included.
read_skill_file.output_schema.properties.content.descrip: The file body. A binary file omits this field and returns only a message.
read_skill_file.output_schema.properties.truncated.descr: Whether the body was truncated for length
read_skill_file.output_schema.properties.message.descrip: Further detail, such as a binary file with no body returned, or a truncation notice

Response format: json or toon. Defaults to toon.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.kn_id.descriptio: Knowledge network id. The X-Kn-ID request header carries it too.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.query.descriptio: A natural-language question or keywords. Pass the whole sentence; there is no need to split it into field conditions, because the vector channel takes the sentence and the full-text channel tokenizes it with an analyzer.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.concept_groups.d: Restrict recall to the named BKN concept groups; without it recall runs across the whole knowledge network.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.object_types.des: Pin recall to these object types. Takes object type ids (for example material), never names. Ids come from concept_id in a search_schema response, object_type_id in a search_instance response, or object_types[].id from get_kn_detail. Without it recall is not restricted. The filter runs before relevance ranking and the max_object_types cut, so a pinned object type cannot be squeezed out by ranking below the cut.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.exclude_object_t: Drop these object types from recall, again by object type id. Use it to re-run a query after a previous call returned object types that turned out to be noise. When an id appears in both this list and object_types, exclusion wins.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.max_object_types: Maximum number of object types that take part in instance recall. Raising it covers more object types, at the cost of one more downstream query per object type. This is a hard cap: concept recall brings back a few more object types to keep its schema self-consistent (it completes relation endpoints), and those still appear under object_types, but no instance query is issued against them.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.max_instances_pe: How many instances to return per object type.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.rerank.descripti: Whether to semantically rerank the recalled results. Off by default. When on, a cross-encoder judges the relevance of each instance against the query and **reorders the returned results** — it can separate cases such as an amount owed from a repayment, which a rank-fusion score cannot. It costs one more model call, roughly 100 to 400ms, and requires the reranking small model to be registered in the deployment; when that model is unavailable the original order is kept and no error is raised. Turn it on for precision, leave it off for speed.
search_instance.input_schema.properties.include_object_t: Whether to include a condensed definition of the object types that were hit, meaning property names and types. Included by default. Turning it off pays off only when you already hold the schema of those object types; otherwise reading the returned instances costs another get_object_types call.
search_instance.output_schema.properties.nodes.descripti: The instances that were hit, grouped by object type, each group ordered by relevance. There is no global ordering across object types, so do not read the order of appearance as which object type is more relevant.
search_instance.output_schema.properties.nodes.items.pro: Id of the object type this instance belongs to, usable directly with get_object_types or query_object_instance.
Instance properties. The field meanings come from the object type definition returned by search_schema or get_object_types.
Relevance score of this instance within its own object type. Scores from different object types are not comparable.

The relevance score from the reranking small model. Present only when instance reranking is enabled in the deployment and the model scored this entry. Reranking changes the returned order, not score: once it is on, consume the results in the order given rather than sorting by score yourself.
search_instance.output_schema.properties.object_types.de: The condensed object type definitions needed to read nodes, **covering only the object types that actually produced instances**, not every object type recall scanned. Absent when include_object_types=false.
search_instance.output_schema.properties.object_types.it: Object type or relation type id. Note that action_types in this tool uses id rather than concept_id.
Name. As above, the action_types entry calls this name.
Description text, usually including the property table of the type.
Bound data resource {type, id, name}; the id works as the {{.<resource_id>}} placeholder in run_sql.
Data properties [{name, type, condition_operations}]; condition_operations decides whether the property can be filtered with match or knn.
search_instance.output_schema.properties.message.descrip: Present only when nothing was hit, explaining why the result is empty.
